n: Habakkuk is unique: instead of speaking for God to the people, he questions God on behalf of the people. He lived in Judah shortly before Babylon’s invasion, around 605 BC — in the same era as Lehi and Jeremiah.

f.g: The name may mean “embrace” or come from a word for a garden plant.

n: Habakkuk’s honest complaint: “Lord, how long must I cry for help before You listen? I cry ‘Violence!’ and You don’t save.” Scripture shows it is okay to bring our hard questions to God.
Why does God make him watch injustice? Everywhere he looks there is destruction, violence, and conflict in Judah.
Because of this, the law is paralyzed and justice never wins. The wicked surround the righteous, so justice comes out twisted.
God answers: Look among the nations and be amazed! I am doing something in your lifetime you wouldn’t believe even if told. Paul quoted this as a warning against rejecting the gospel.

f.w: I will work a work in your days

n: The surprise: God is raising up the Chaldeans (Babylonians) — a fierce, swift nation that will sweep through the land seizing homes that aren’t theirs. God uses even pagan powers to discipline His people.

f.g: The ruling people of the Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar.

n: They are terrifying and answer to no one; they make their own rules and honor only themselves.

f.w: their judgment and their dignity shall proceed of themselves
f.g: They are a law unto themselves.

n: Their horses are faster than leopards and fiercer than wolves hunting at dusk. Their cavalry swoops in from far away like eagles diving on prey.

f.g: Wolves hungry after a day without food, hunting at dusk.

f.w: they shall fly as the eagle

n: They come intent on violence, sweeping forward like the desert wind, gathering captives as countless as sand.

f.w: their faces shall sup up as the east wind
f.g: Their faces press forward like a scorching desert wind.

n: They laugh at kings and scoff at fortresses, simply piling up earth ramps to capture them.

f.g: Build siege ramps of earth against city walls.

n: They sweep on like the wind, but they are guilty — they make their own strength their god.

f.w: imputing this his power unto his god
f.g: Treating their own might as divine.

n: Habakkuk responds: Lord, You are eternal and holy. We will not die. You have appointed Babylon to correct us, our Rock.

f.g: Ancient scribes say the original read “You do not die”; either way it affirms God’s eternal nature.
Literally “O Rock” — a title of steadfast strength.

n: His deeper question: You are too pure to look on evil, so how can You stay silent while the wicked swallow up people more righteous than they?

f.w: Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil

n: God seems to treat people like fish or bugs with no leader to protect them.
The Babylonians haul in nations like a fisherman with hooks and nets — and they rejoice over their catch.
They worship their nets — their military power — because it makes them rich and well-fed.
Will they keep emptying their nets and killing nations forever? Habakkuk’s question hangs, awaiting God’s answer in chapter 2.
